item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=Can+falsification+of+core+reward-scalarization+assumptions+be+automated+in+reinforcement+learning+architectures%3F&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6836287\", \"title\": [\"Research on Trajectory Planning for Automated Vehicles Based on Reinforcement Learning in Sparse Reward Environments\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Trajectory planning for automated vehicles in complex and dynamic environments is the core issue of automated driving systems. Dynamic obstacles and nonlinear road conditions in complicated traffic scenarios pose severe challenges to the stability and adaptability of planning algorithms. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning fails to converge efficiently under sparse reward conditions, resulting in low learning efficiency and unstable trajectories. To solve the above problems, this paper proposes a reinforcement learning-based trajectory planning model for automated vehicles, namely the Intrinsic Curiosity Module–Progress Hindsight Experience Replay (ICM-PHER). This model introduces an intrinsic reward mechanism driven by prediction error to facilitate effective exploration, thereby alleviating training inefficiency caused by sparse rewards. Combined with curriculum learning, a dynamic target point guidance strategy is designed to enable vehicles to learn gradually from simple tasks to complex ones. Furthermore, an improved Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) mechanism integrated with a dynamic filtering sampler is adopted to remove low-quality experiences and improve the utilization efficiency of valid samples. A multi-scenario automated driving simulation platform is established to verify the performance of the proposed model. Experimental results show that compared with baseline methods, the ICM-PHER model delivers up to 300% higher average reward in sparse reward and complex scenarios, reduces training collisions by about 60%, and increases key indicators including speed and trajectory length by 23%–230%. The proposed method greatly boosts exploration efficiency and trajectory planning performance, and effectively improves the trajectory planning efficiency and complex environment adaptability of automated vehicles in sparse reward settings.</jats:p>\", …

The proposed method greatly boosts exploration efficiency and trajectory planning performance, and effectively improves the trajectory planning efficiency and complex environment adaptability of automated vehicles in sparse reward settings.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6836287\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202610.1802.v1\", \"title\": [\"Automated Dense Reward Function Design for Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Driving\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Crafting reward functions remains a challenge in reinforcement learning, particularly in autonomous driving (AD), where safety, efficiency, and task completion must be balanced. We introduce a GPT-5.6-based revision of AD Reward Designer, a framework for generating interpretable dense reward functions from natural language goals and concise Pythonic environment descriptions. The initial reward generation requires no expert demonstrations or model fine-tuning. GPT-5.6 translates task requirements into executable reward code, which is checked before being used by a reinforcement learning algorithm. Policy rollout summaries and human feedback then guide iterative refinement of the reward terms and their weights. An optional demonstration-conditioned extension supplies expert and policy trajectories as additional context for reward design. We retain Highway-env and MetaDrive as the evaluation environments and PPO as the policy learning algorithm. The original experiments provide evidence for the feasibility of language-model-generated rewards; their numerical results are retained as historical evidence and are not reported as GPT-5.6 measurements. The revised GPT-5.6 configuration requires a new evaluation under the same task settings.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202610.1802.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 10, 20]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.4024901\", \"title\": [\"Reward Is Not Enough: Can We Liberate AI From the Reinforcement Learning Paradigm?\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>I present arguments against the hypothesis put forward by Silver, Singh, Precup, and Sutton: reward maximization is not enough to explain many activities associated with natural and artificial intelligence including knowledge, learning, perception, social intelligence, evolution, language, generalisation and imitation. <br><br>I show such reductio ad lucrum has its intellectual origins in the political economy of Homo economicus and substantially overlaps with the radical version of behaviourism. <br><br>I show why the reinforcement learning paradigm, despite its demonstrable usefulness in some practical application, is an incomplete framework for intelligence -- natural and artificial.<br><br>Complexities of intelligent behaviour are not simply second-order complications on top of reward maximisation. This fact has profound implications for the development of practically usable, smart, safe and robust artificially intelligent agents.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4024901\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.3901/jme.2024.10.245\", \"title\": [\"Bayesian Inverse Reinforcement Learning-based Reward Learning for Automated Driving\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.3901/jme.2024.10.245\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2024]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "5394664325d0715979337aab766a83022f41ab38158fc7cf32df75604ff6a949", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6836287", "doi:10.20944/preprints202610.1802.v1", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.4024901", "doi:10.3901/jme.2024.10.245"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6836287", "https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202610.1802.v1", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4024901", "https://doi.org/10.3901/jme.2024.10.245"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
